sections.title: The Convert's Inheritance from His Non-Jewish Parents
sections.html: The Sages said: "A convert who has converted is like (damei) a newborn child" (Yevamot 22a), that is, from a legal standpoint, at the time of his conversion the convert's connection to his family members lapses. And so the law is regarding inheritance. Before the conversion, the convert would inherit his father, for the descendants of Noaḥ (benei Noaḥ) inherit their parents by Torah law. But when the convert chose to convert, he is like one who has been born anew, and therefore, without an explicit will of his non-Jewish parents granting him of their estate, by Torah law the convert does not inherit them. But the Sages were concerned that there might be converts who, in order to gain the inheritance, would revert to their old ways and conduct themselves as non-Jews; therefore they enacted that even without an explicit will converts inherit their non-Jewish parents (Kiddushin 17b; SA ḤM 283:1).1

sections.title: The Convert's Property After His Death
sections.html:
Since a convert who has converted is considered like a newborn child, his legal ties to his family have been severed, and therefore, if he died without leaving a will, his relatives from before the conversion do not inherit him. And since he has no heirs, upon his death all his property and all the debts owed to him become ownerless (hefker), and whoever is first to acquire them acquires them. And even if he converted with his children or with his brothers, they do not inherit him, since at the time of the conversion they are like ones born anew, and their family ties that are binding with regard to inheritance are void. Even a child who was born after the conversion, if his conception was before the conversion, does not inherit him, for regarding the inheritance tie with the father, the determining time is the beginning of the pregnancy; therefore, upon the death of his convert father, all his property becomes ownerless, and whoever is first to acquire it acquires it (Bava Batra 149a; SA ḤM 275:1).

From this halakha too we learn about the special status of the convert, in whom the power of choice is most prominent, and the natural arrangements of inheritance do not apply to him. And if he wants his children who converted with him to inherit him, he must choose this and write a will that will arrange it as a gift that he decided to give them one hour before his death.

However, in practice, today, as a result of the law, the convert's children or his biological relatives acquire his property even if he did not write a will, for since upon his death his property becomes ownerless, and according to the law only his children or relatives are entitled to use his property, they are the ones who acquire his property from the ownerless state. And if he has no children or relatives, the law establishes that the state acquires his property.

If the convert fathered another child after his conversion, since according to the Torah that child is his only heir, it does not help that according to the law his children who were born before his conversion are in possession of his property; and if he wants all his children to inherit him, he must write this in a will. Likewise, when the deceased is a Jew who fathered children from a non-Jewish woman who afterward converted together with them, according to halakha only his relatives who are Jewish from birth, such as his brothers, inherit him. And if he wants his convert children to acquire his property according to halakha, he will need to write a will that will arrange the distribution of his property.2

sections.title: Returning a Convert's Loan to His Children
sections.html: The Sages said in the Mishna (Shevi'it 10:9): "One who borrows from a convert whose sons converted with him – he need not return it to his sons, but if he returned it, the Sages are pleased with him." That is, a Jew who received a loan from a convert whose sons also converted with him, and afterward the convert died, is not obligated to return the debt of the loan to his convert sons, since when they converted they became like ones born anew, and they do not inherit their father. But if he returns the loan to his sons, the Sages are pleased with him, because he is conducting himself according to integrity and morality. However, there are situations in which, if he returns it, the Sages are not pleased with him, and the Rishonim disagreed as to which circumstances are being discussed (Kiddushin 17b). But since in practice, if he does not return the loan to the convert's children a ḥillul Hashem (desecration of God's name) will be caused, it is a mitzva to return the loan to them, in order to sanctify the name of Heaven and prevent a desecration of God's name. And the same law applies to returning a deposit and anything similar.3

sections.title: The Convert's Obligation to Honor His Non-Jewish Parents
sections.html:
It is a mitzva for the convert to honor his non-Jewish parents, and it is forbidden for him to disgrace them (Rambam, Hilkhot Mamrim 5:11; SA YD 241:9). And although the mitzva of honoring parents, with its stringent parameters, does not apply to him, in everything that natural morality requires, the convert too is obligated toward his parents. And if he goes further and honors them more than natural morality requires, each place according to what is accepted there, he will thereby have hiddur mitzva (an enhancement of the mitzva). But if his parents are liable to influence him or his children for the worse, he should honor them as natural morality requires and no more (see the next halakha).

Since accepted morality obligates all human beings, Ḥam was therefore punished for disgracing Noaḥ his father (Bereishit 9:25). And when a person goes further and honors his parents more than accepted morality requires, he has merit in this, as is told of Dama ben Netina, who was a Roman official and was very careful about honoring his father, not to wake him even for the sake of selling precious stones at a very high price. And God gave him his reward, in that a red heifer (para aduma) was born in his herd and he could have received an enormous sum for it, but since he did not want to benefit from the reward for honoring his father, he was satisfied with the sum he would have received for the precious stones (Kiddushin 31a).

And although the convert is considered like one born anew, this does not mean that he is exempt from his previous obligations; rather, he has risen to a higher and more sanctified level. Therefore all the obligations that natural morality imposes on him remain upon him. Not only that, but if after he converts he violates them, there will be a desecration of God's name in this, for people will say that the one converting went "from a more stringent holiness to a lesser holiness": while he was a non-Jew he was obligated to honor his parents, whereas when he converted he was exempted from his obligation, as if the holiness of the Torah of Israel obligates less than the holiness of the morality accepted among the nations. And so we find with Avraham Avinu, who by the command of the Creator left his father and went up to the Land of Israel, and the Sages said (Bereishit Rabba 39:7) that he was worried and said: "If I go out and leave my father, people will desecrate the name of Heaven through me and say: 'He left his father and went away in his old age.'" Therefore it is stated (Bereishit 12:1): "And the Lord said to Avram: Go forth from your land and from your birthplace and from your father's house, to the land that I will show you." "The Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: Lekh lekha (go forth for yourself) – I exempt you from honoring father and mother, but I do not exempt another from honoring father and mother." That is, because of the importance of the mitzva of going up to the Land, God exempted him from his obligation toward his father. And some added that Avraham was exempt from honoring his father because Teraḥ his father was wicked, for he did not agree to join in faith in the one God, and under Nimrod's pressure he even agreed to hand his son over to the fiery furnace; and nevertheless Avraham Avinu was concerned about a desecration of God's name, and God instructed him to go up to the Land (Ḥida, Devash Le-fi 1:39; Panim Yafot, Bereishit 12:1).

Therefore, it is forbidden for the convert to disgrace his parents, and all the more so it is forbidden for him to strike them. And it is a mitzva for him to treat them with respect, and to help them in their illness or old age, as accepted morality requires.4

sections.title: Further Matters in Honoring Parents
sections.html:
Sometimes the convert's parents weaken him in his new path as a Jew, and sometimes the convert is not worried for himself, but is worried that his parents will influence his children. In such situations, it is proper for the convert to set his residence far from them, and thus, without hurting his parents, he will distance himself and his children from their influence. And if he is worried that even during visits with them they will influence his children for the worse, he should reduce the visits to the point at which he will still not be considered ungrateful toward them. And if they are hostile to him because of his conversion, he may refrain from visiting them at all, and only if they need help in their illness should he assist them as accepted morality requires. And if they are ill and ask to see their grandchildren before their death, it is proper for him to travel with his children to visit them (see Igrot Moshe YD 2:130).

When the convert's parents live abroad, it is a mitzva for the convert to make aliya to the Land like all of Israel, and thereby the concern that his parents will influence his children for the worse will be removed. Nevertheless, in special cases, if the convert has the means for it, it is proper for him to travel to visit them, for example when one of them is ill or when a special celebration is being held for him [?].

When the convert's parents are ill, even though they believe in another religion, it is fitting for their son to pray for their recovery. And if they wish it, it is fitting that he even ask the gabbai to say a "Mi She-berakh" for their recovery.5

If the convert's parents take an interest in Judaism, it is good for him to bring them closer to the mitzvot of the Torah. And if they are happy to participate with him in Shabbat meals, it is good to include them in the meals. In this way, the concern that the parents will influence the grandchildren for the worse diminishes, and on the contrary, it is even possible that they will encourage the grandchildren to cleave to Judaism and the mitzvot of the Torah.

sections.title: Mourning
sections.html:
The mitzva that obligates mourning for first-degree relatives applies only to Jews. Therefore, even when an entire family converted together, since everyone who converts is like one born anew, their previous family ties do not obligate them to mourn for one another (Rambam, Hilkhot Evel 2:3; SA and Rema YD 374:5). All the more so, the convert is not obligated to mourn for his non-Jewish relatives. Likewise, a Jew whose Jewish father fathered children from a non-Jewish woman is not obligated to mourn for his brothers who are not Jewish.

But all this is from the standpoint of obligation; if he wishes, the convert may mourn for his non-Jewish parents or brothers as is accepted among them, and if he wishes to sit shiva for them according to the custom of Israel, he may. And when his friends know that one of his relatives has died, and if he continues to work and conduct himself as usual it will be an affront to the honor of the deceased, it is fitting that he mourn for him as is accepted.

When his parents or brothers also converted, although he is not obligated to mourn for them, it is fitting that he honor them and sit shiva for them, and observe all the customs of mourning for them, from keri'a (tearing the garment) to the mourning of the thirty days and the year.

It is proper for the convert to say the Mourner's Kaddish for his parents in the year of their death. And even if they did not convert, it is fitting that he show gratitude to them for having given birth to him by saying Kaddish for the elevation of their souls. And all the more so, if they converted with him, it is a mitzva for him to say Kaddish for the elevation of their souls.6

sections.title: Peru U-revu
sections.html:
A convert who fathered children before his conversion has fulfilled through them the mitzva of peru u-revu (be fruitful and multiply). And although the descendants of Noaḥ are not obligated in the mitzva of peru u-revu as Israel is, the descendants of Noaḥ have a mitzva to engage in the settlement of the world, so that the world will endure and develop and not be desolate, as it is stated (Yeshayahu 45:18): "He did not create it to be a waste; He formed it to be inhabited." And God blessed Noaḥ and his descendants that they would fulfill this mitzva and be fruitful and multiply, as it is stated (Bereishit 9:1): "And God blessed Noaḥ and his sons, and said to them: Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth." And since he fulfilled the mitzva to settle the world, he has in practice also fulfilled the mitzva of peru u-revu. And although from a halakhic-legal standpoint a convert who has converted is considered like a newborn child, in the mitzva of settling the world one follows nature, and from the standpoint of nature the children he fathered while still a non-Jew are his children, and therefore he has fulfilled through them the mitzva of peru u-revu.

Some say that even if his children did not convert, he has fulfilled through them the mitzva of peru u-revu (Maharil, and so it emerges from other Rishonim). And some say that only if they converted has he fulfilled through them the mitzva of peru u-revu (Rambam; SA EH 1:7).7

But a Jew who fathered children from a non-Jewish woman has not fulfilled through them the mitzva of peru u-revu, because they are non-Jews and their lineage does not follow him. And some say that if they convert, they will thereby rectify his sin and he will fulfill through them the mitzva of peru u-revu.8

sections.title: Prohibitions of Forbidden Relations for Converts
sections.html:
The Sages said: "A convert who has converted is like a newborn child" (Yevamot 22a). That is, from a legal standpoint, at the time of his conversion the convert's connection to his family members lapses. Therefore the severe death penalties that apply to those who sin in forbidden relations (gilui arayot) with family relatives do not apply to him. But the prohibition itself remains in place, for all the relatives who were forbidden to him within the framework of the seven commandments of the descendants of Noaḥ remain forbidden to him even after the conversion. For example, a brother and sister who converted: since they were forbidden to marry while they were non-Jews, even after their conversion they are forbidden to marry. For it is impossible that as a result of their elevation to the holiness of Israel, something that was forbidden to them as non-Jews should now become permitted; for if so, there would be a desecration of God's name in this, for people would say: "We have come from a more stringent holiness to a lesser holiness!"

In addition, the Sages forbade the convert to marry a female relative who was not forbidden to him while he was a non-Jew, if there is concern that as a result people will mistakenly think that it is permitted for Israel as well. For example, a non-Jew is permitted to marry his brother's divorcée, whereas among Israel this is forbidden; and the Sages forbade the convert to marry the divorcée of his convert brother, so that people will not mistakenly think that it is permitted for Israel as well.9

sections.title: A Convert Woman and a Kohen
sections.html:
There are special mitzvot for kohanim, in order to set them apart and sanctify them for the holy service. Among the prohibitions specific to kohanim is that a kohen may not marry a divorced woman or a woman who had relations with a man whom she is forbidden to marry (zona). As it is stated (Vayikra 21:6-7): "They shall be holy to their God, and they shall not profane the name of their God, for the fire-offerings of the Lord, the bread of their God, they offer, and they shall be holy. A woman who is a zona or profaned (ḥalala) they shall not take, and a woman divorced from her husband they shall not take, for he is holy to his God." The Sages learned that a convert woman too is included among the women forbidden to kohanim, since she was not preserved in the holiness of Israel (Yevamot 60b; 61a; SA EH 6:8).

But a daughter of converts whose conception and birth were in holiness is fit to marry a kohen. However, after the Temple was destroyed and the Sanhedrin, which dealt with clarifying the lineage of the kohanim, ceased, the kohanim adopted the practice of being stringent with themselves and refrained from marrying a woman who is a descendant of converts on both sides. But if a kohen married a daughter of converts, they are not instructed to divorce, since by the letter of the law it is permitted (Kiddushin 78b; SA EH 7:21).10

sections.title: The Father's Name in the Ketuba
sections.html:
The custom is to write in the ketuba of converts: "So-and-so son of Avraham Avinu" or "So-and-so daughter of Avraham Avinu." But if the groom or the bride converted with their parents at a young age, and they are embarrassed and want the name of their father, who begot them and converted with them and raised them, to be written in the ketuba, one may le-khatḥila write his name.

Similarly, parents who adopted a child and converted him, and the child or his adoptive father are embarrassed at having it written in the ketuba that he is the son of "Avraham Avinu," one may le-khatḥila write in the ketuba the name of his adoptive father.11

sections.title: His Father's Name for Being Called to the Torah
sections.html:
According to the custom of those of Ashkenazic origin and some of those of Sephardic origin, when a person is called up to the Torah, he is called by his name and his father's name, for example: "Reuven son of Ya'akov," and the custom is that if he is a convert, he is called "Reuven son of Avraham," after Avraham Avinu, who is the father of all converts (Rema OḤ 139:3). Similarly, when the gabbai or the rabbi says a "Mi She-berakh" for one called up to the Torah, the custom is that he mentions his name and his father's name, and if he is a convert, the custom is to say "son of Avraham."

However, when this causes distress to the convert or to his father, he should be called by the name of the father who raised him. For example, if the one called up to the Torah converted with his parents, and he does not want anyone to understand from this that he is a convert. Or his father may be pained at his name not being mentioned, for after he begot him and raised him, and brought him to convert with him, he wants him to be mentioned as his father. Likewise, when parents adopted a non-Jewish infant, the adoptive father may be pained that after all the effort he invested in raising and educating his son, the son is not called by his name. In all these cases, one should mention the name of the father who begot him and converted with him, or who adopted him.12
